Second, in September 2025, Cambodia witnessed the passage of an amendment to the law on nationality, enabling the national authorities to revoke the birth citizenship of Cambodians found guilty of colluding with foreign powers to undermine the country. The alarm has been sounded by civil society and other stakeholders that this amendment is an intimidating instrument to constrain dissident voices internally and externally. The preferred approach is thus to refrain from applying this law and to orient towards its revocation. This leads appropriately to the findings of the most recent report on the human rights situation. A constructive feature is that the national authorities are committed to multilateralism. Yet, there is the quandary that the national system remains in the hands of the established elite, In particular since 2017, when the main opposition party, the Cambodian National Rescue Party, was disbanded by court order under dubious circumstances. The current rulers are closely aligned with the political party that won the largest share of votes in various elections, which were neither free nor fair, and there has been a monopolistic transfer of power from one generation to the next of the same kith and kin. The situation is aggravated by the following elements. First, in 2023 and 2024, three elections were held at different levels in the country. All were distorted in favor of the ruling elite. Second, political actors continue to be detained, and there have been new arrests, detentions, and prosecutions of opposition members. Third, various civil society actors, such as environmental and human rights defenders, were harassed, arrested, detained, and sentenced to imprisonment during this reporting period. Judicialized lawfare casts a wide shadow over those perceived to be dissidents, with the justice system being used to apply laws and policies to sanction decisions from the top. Fourth, there were multiple cases of transnational repression during the year. And fifth, there were many cases of online fraud, scams, and related trafficking in persons. The situation remains serious, with a clampdown in one place resulting in a pop-up in another place. Turning now to the issue of natural resources, the country is not short of laws and policies on this front. In practice, however, there is a quagmire of potholes. The issue of local stakeholders demands a participatory response to ensure a more democratic process of resource management, conservation, and benefit sharing, rather than unwittingly placing them in the hands of politically linked tycoons. Interconnected challenges include forced evictions, land tenure and dispossession, respect or disrespect for the principle of free, prior, and informed consent and related remedies, and for indigenous peoples and their rights, together with predatory microfinance and debt and reprisals against stakeholders. There's also a need for the business sector to cooperate to integrate human rights due diligence into their activities. Lessons from those life elements call for not only detailed plans and laws on natural resources, but also the space for political liberalization, action against strategic lawsuits, constraining public participation, localized stakeholdership, responsiveness from the government and related businesses, and people-led checks and balances against abuse of power.
